html:
SMTO-GWT-0076 — The GPU action took too long to finish

GUID: 78c0d2a1-ff8a-5c18-92bd-c1d95154e477
Slug: gpu-operation-timeout
Domain: GWT · Subsystem: gpu

What happened

  • SMTO stopped waiting because this GPU action ran out of time. If it was a settings change, it may or may not have happened, and NVIDIA's tool might still be running.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Wait a minute, then ask SMTO to show the current details for this GPU, without asking for any change. This gives a slow NVIDIA tool time to finish and shows whether a power, persistence or compute mode change took effect.
  2. Only if the details still show the old value, ask SMTO for the change again. Don't repeat clock or reset requests. Repeating a change that already happened could disturb the card, and clock or reset results can't be confirmed by a reading.
  3. If even the GPU details time out, ask the person who manages that computer to check that the NVIDIA driver responds. When a simple reading also runs out of time, the driver or card is likely stuck, and further requests won't help.

What success looks like

  • The GPU details load normally and show the setting you wanted.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages the computer with the GPU. Don't keep resending the change while the card is slow to respond.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • A GPU operation reached its deadline (45 s ordinary, 330 s sampling, 5 s per nvidia-smi invocation) before completion was confirmed, or cleanup of a timed-out read could not confirm that the nvidia-smi process ended.

What this means

  • A GPU checkpoint reached its operation deadline, or subprocess cleanup could not confirm timely termination on a read path. The retained phase, target and receipt determine what executed. Rendering this definition adds no probe, retries, dispatch or changes to resource ownership.

Why this can happen

  • A GPU checkpoint reached its operation deadline, or subprocess cleanup could not confirm timely termination on a read path.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect phase, active_execution_possible and retained result; separate an unstarted configuration prerequisite from an attempted device change.

How to fix it

  • Check the receipt's active_execution_possible flag and the Gateway job named gpu_ plus the execution ID; on the Gateway host confirm nvidia-smi responds (for example nvidia-smi -q completes) and no stuck nvidia-smi process remains. Read gpu.device for the UUID and reconcile any attempted configuration before issuing another mutation.
  • Inspect the original operation and provider state. Reconcile any attempted configuration before further mutation.

Retry and execution caution

  • For a mutation, inspect the exact UUID and resolve any active execution or uncertain effect before issuing a new operation. Never replay a reset or an unobservable clock change to infer its result.

How to verify the fix

  • The existing operation is settled and provider availability is established before another justified read or mutation.

What not to do

  • Do not replay uncertain mutations, kill GPU clients automatically or invent sensor values.

Technical notes

  • The retained phase, target and receipt determine what executed. Rendering this definition adds no probe, retries, dispatch or changes to resource ownership.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
